prompts.title: Your country's recommendations dashboard
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

## Goal
A dashboard for a diplomat, NGO or NHRI staff member to see at a glance what UN human rights mechanisms have said to Kenya: how much, when, on which themes, and to find the exact paragraphs quickly.

## The data
File `WORKSHOP_DATA.uhri`; the country name is read from its `country` field, never typed in. Fields used: `date`, `year`, `body`, `mechanism`, `type`, `symbol`, `doc_url`, `text`, `themes`, `sdgs`, `affected_persons`, plus `sdg_names` for the SDG filter labels.

## What the app shows
1. Title "UN human rights recommendations to [country]", then one line: source, total number of records, earliest–latest year, all read from the file.
2. A filter bar: dropdown for mechanism; dropdown for body (treaty body or mandate); two boxes for first and last year; dropdown for SDG (number and name); a keyword box; a "Reset" button. Any change updates everything below at once.
3. A line "Showing X of Y records" plus a plain description of the active filters (e.g. "Treaty bodies · 2015–2020 · keyword: torture").
4. A horizontal bar chart of the 10 most frequent themes among the matching records, longest bar on top, each labelled with its count. Note below: "A record with several items is counted once for each."
5. A table of matching records, newest first: date, body, symbol (linked to the UN document, new tab), first line of the text. The recommending State is not shown as a separate column. Clicking a row expands it to show the full paragraph with its themes and SDGs; clicking again closes it. 100 rows at a time, with "Show more".

## Rules for the code
- Total and year range come from counting all records and taking the smallest and largest `year`.
- A record matches when it passes every active filter; keyword search is case-insensitive on `text`. Only recommendations and concerns/observations are counted anywhere.
- Chart: for each matching record add one per item in its list; sort by count, keep the top 10, break ties alphabetically.
- Text stays verbatim: the first line is `text` up to its first line break or 160 characters plus "…"; the expanded view is the full `text`, unchanged.
- Every row links `symbol` to `doc_url`. Missing `doc_url`: symbol shown unlinked. Missing `symbol`: "(no symbol)".
- Missing `date`: "date unknown", sorted last. Missing `body`: "unknown". Empty `themes` or `sdgs`: "none recorded" in the expanded row; such records simply do not appear in the chart.
- No matches: show "No records match these filters" instead of an empty chart.

## How we will know it works
1. On load, the title names your country and "Showing X of Y" has X equal to Y.
2. Choose "Universal Periodic Review": the count, chart and table change together, and no row shows a treaty body like CEDAW or CRC.
3. Type a rare word: the count drops and every visible row contains that word when expanded.
4. Click a symbol: a docs.un.org page opens in a new tab with the same symbol.
5. Click a row: the full paragraph appears word for word, including its paragraph number.

## Not in this version
- No comparison with other countries or with the global average.
- No tracking of whether a recommendation was accepted, noted or implemented.
- No AI summaries or translations; every word on screen comes from the file.
- No export to Excel or PDF.
prompts.problem: I need to see what UN human rights mechanisms have told my country, on which themes and when, find the exact paragraphs fast, and know whether I can trust the numbers.

prompts.title: Paragraphs out of a PDF
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

## Goal
A checking tool for anyone who quotes a UN document paragraph by paragraph. It splits the raw PDF text of E/C.12/GC/27 into its numbered paragraphs and shows where the converter damaged the text, so the reader can verify the split before relying on it.

## The data
`WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`: `title`, `symbol`, `doc_url` and `source` for the heading and links; `records` (`page`, `text`) is the text to split; `reference.paragraphs`, `reference.footnotes` and `reference.first_words` are the answer key.

## What the app shows
1. Title and symbol linked to `doc_url`, with one line: "raw PDF text, N pages, source: …" (N from the data).
2. Three counters: paragraphs found / paragraphs in the reference; footnotes removed / footnotes in the reference; paragraphs whose opening words differ from the reference. Under them: "Found by the code from the page text; reference figures come from the file."
3. A table, one row per paragraph: number, page where it starts, first line (about 90 characters), symbol linked to `doc_url`, and a "Differs" mark where the opening words do not match. A tick box "Show differences first" moves marked rows to the top. Clicking a row opens the full paragraph beneath it, exactly as extracted, with the reference's first words shown beside it.
4. A "Download CSV" button.
5. A collapsed list "Lines removed as headers, footers and footnotes", so the reader can see nothing substantive was discarded.

## Rules for the code
- Join the pages in order. Remove lines that are only a page number, only the document symbol, or a distribution code ("GE." followed by digits).
- Footnote lines (a small number then text, at the foot of a page) are removed from the paragraphs and only counted.
- A paragraph starts where a line begins with the next expected number, a full stop and a space ("1. ", then "2. " …). Numbers out of sequence (years, cross-references) do not start a paragraph. Text runs until the next start.
- Lettered sub-paragraphs stay inside their numbered paragraph.
- "Differs" means the paragraph's first six words are not the reference's, comparing word by word while ignoring case, punctuation and extra spaces. If the reference has no entry for a number, show "no reference", not "Differs".
- Paragraph text is never edited or paraphrased, only displayed.
- The CSV holds number, page, whether it matches the reference, and the full text with values quoted, built and saved in the browser.

## How we will know it works
- The first counter reads "N of 90" (90 is the reference count in the file), with N close to it.
- The table numbers run 1, 2, 3 … without gaps, and at least 30 rows appear.
- Clicking row 1 shows text starting "A clean, healthy and sustainable environment".
- Every row marked "Differs" shows the reference words it was compared with.
- The downloaded CSV opens in a spreadsheet with as many rows as the table.

## Not in this version
- It flags damage; it does not repair text or reorder paragraphs.
- Only this document; no upload of other PDFs.
- No comparison with other language versions.
prompts.problem: Our office copies paragraphs out of UN PDFs by hand. Can a tool split a General Comment into its numbered paragraphs and footnotes, and show me where it got things wrong?

prompts.title: Verbatim finder for General Comments
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

## Goal
A search tool for people drafting submissions, reports or briefs who need to find and cite exactly what a treaty body said in a General Comment. Type a search, find the real paragraph, copy a correct citation.

## The data
`WORKSHOP_DATA.gc`, one record per paragraph. Fields used: `text` (searched and displayed), `committee`, `year`, `symbol`, `paragraph`, `short_title`, `doc_url`. `title` is used only when `short_title` is empty. `id` and `cited_articles` are not used.

## What the app shows
1. Title "General Comments search" and one line: source, number of paragraphs, year range, all read from the data.
2. Search box with a Search button (Enter also searches) and a one-line help: words are combined with AND unless you write OR; NOT excludes a word; "quotes" find an exact phrase. Example: `"best interests" AND child`.
3. Two filters: committee (every committee in the data, plus "All") and year (from–to). Changing a filter re-runs the search.
4. A count line: "N paragraphs match out of M, filters: …".
5. A small bar chart: matching paragraphs per committee for the current search, with a "How this is computed" note.
6. Results, sorted newest General Comment first. Each card: committee, short title, year, the symbol linked to `doc_url` (new tab); then the full paragraph, with the search words highlighted; and a "Copy citation" button that copies the symbol and paragraph only, e.g. "CCPR/C/GC/37, para. 12". The button reads "Copied" for two seconds.
7. If nothing matches: "No paragraph contains these words" and a tip to try OR or fewer words.

## Rules for the code
- The search looks at the paragraph text only. Matching is case-insensitive. A plain word matches a whole word ("right" does not match "rights"); a quoted phrase matches that exact sequence of words. Words separated by spaces are ANDed; OR joins alternatives; NOT before a word or phrase excludes it.
- Filters are applied first, then the search. N, the chart bars and the cards come from the same list, so the bars add up to N.
- `text` is shown character for character; highlighting only wraps the matched words and never changes, trims or summarises them.
- The citation is `symbol` + ", para. " + `paragraph`, nothing invented.
- Missing values: no `short_title` → show `title`, else the symbol; no `year` → show "year unknown", included when the year filter is open, excluded by a from–to range; no `doc_url` → symbol unlinked; empty `text` → never matches but still counted in M.

## How we will know it works
1. Search `"best interests" AND child`: every card highlights both "best interests" and "child"; the number of cards equals N.
2. Search `torture NOT detention`: no card contains the word "detention".
3. Choose CRC in the committee filter: the chart shows a single bar whose height equals N.
4. Click Copy citation, paste into a text editor: you get the card's own symbol and paragraph, e.g. `CRC/C/GC/14, para. 6`.
5. Click a symbol: the UN document opens in a new tab.

## Not in this version
- No brackets for grouping searches, no wildcards, no stemming ("right" and "rights" are different words).
- No export of all results to a file.
- No saved or shared searches.

prompts.title: A research wiki on neurotechnology and justice
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

## Goal
A research wiki for diplomats and NGO, NHRI and UN staff: what nine documents say about one concept in neurotechnology and justice, every quote opening its original page.

## The data
`WORKSHOP_DATA.library`, one record per document: `id`, `symbol`, `kind`, `author`, `year`, `short_title`, `url`; from each of its `passages`: `id`, `page`, `page_label`, `paragraph`, `section`, `text`.

## What the app shows
1. Sidebar: the concept pages with passage counts: mental privacy, freedom of thought, self-incrimination, lie detection, consent, neural data, data solidarity, proportionality. Below, "Add a concept": type a term, press Enter.
2. Page heading: the concept and the terms that find it (lie detection also "deception detection", "brain fingerprinting").
3. Table "Passages by kind of document": one row per `kind`, and a total.
4. The passages, grouped by document, in library order. Group heading: `short_title`, `kind`, `year`, `symbol` linked to `url`. Each passage: its citation as a link calling `studio.openSource(id, page)`, the `section` if any, the `text` folded after three lines.
5. "Related concepts": other concepts found in the same passages, as links.
6. Button "Draft a summary": sends at most the first 12 passages on the page with `await studio.ask(prompt)`; the answer appears in a box labelled "Written by AI. N passages were sent to the model and left the browser".

## Rules for the code
- A passage uses a concept when its `text` contains one of the terms, ignoring case and line breaks. Table, groups, sidebar and related concepts use the same list.
- `text` is shown character for character; the fold hides, never shortens.
- Citation: `symbol` + ", para. " + `paragraph` when `paragraph` is set; otherwise author, year and printed page, e.g. "Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471". Journal articles are cited by surnames ("Szoszkiewicz & Yuste"; "Prainsack et al." for three or more), other documents by `author` as written. `openSource` gets `page`, never `page_label`.
- The prompt lists the passages with their citations and asks for three sentences, each ending with the citation it rests on; the model may rest on only the passages it was sent. The answer sits inside `data-source="ai"`; never called on page load.
- No `symbol` → show `author`; no `section` → omitted; no passages → "No passage uses this term", no button.

## How we will know it works
1. Click "mental privacy": the table rows add up to its total; the Journal article row is not zero.
2. Click "A/81/351, para. N": the PDF opens where that paragraph starts.
3. Open "lie detection": one passage contains "deception detection" but not "lie detection".
4. Click "Draft a summary": three sentences, each ending with a citation also on the page; the label says how many were sent.

## Not in this version
- No adding terms to an existing concept; added concepts are lost on reload.
- No synonyms: "consent" finds "consented", not "agreement".
prompts.problem: Our team keeps losing track of what each report says about neurotechnology in the justice system. Build us a research wiki we can ask questions of, add new reports to, and trust: every quote checked against its source.
